Iceland 5-Day Itinerary: 3 Ideas, From Someone Who’s Visited 8 Times

I’ll be honest with you right from the start… 5 days in Iceland is not enough to see the whole country. You won’t even get close to it. To give you an idea of what I mean, I once went on a 10-day trip around the entire Ring Road and Snæfellsnes Peninsula. During that period, we drove over 1,800 miles in total. Trying to do that in half the time without burning out is pretty much impossible. 

-ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW-

At the same time, you can absolutely have a great adventure with just 5 days on your itinerary. I have been to Iceland eight times in total, some of which have been for precisely this amount of time. Knowing what I could cover and what I had to skip made these trips worthwhile, and I think it would be a shame to ignore Iceland just because you can’t see everything in one go. 

While you will need to make some trade-offs, you can easily still come back with some amazing memories. Today, I will share three options for a 5-day itinerary in Iceland. I’ve visited the country for this length of time in the winter, the off-season, and the summer, so I know what differences and challenges each one poses. 

These itineraries will give you a realistic idea of what you can see and do, and you can customize them based on your own interests and the weather when you arrive. Besides showing you how to spend each day, I’ll also share some of my top tips to help your trip go more smoothly in general.

  • Itinerary #1: My Full 5-Day Summer and Shoulder-Season Itinerary
  • Itinerary #2: A 5-Day Iceland Itinerary Without a Car
  • Itinerary #3: A 5-Day Winter Itinerary
  • Even if You Only Have 5 Days in Iceland, You Can Still Have a Great Time

Itinerary #1: My Full 5-Day Summer and Shoulder-Season Itinerary

When: Late April to mid-October; season may be shorter depending on weather

Where You’ll Stay:

Vík (2 Nights; Book Accommodation)

Snæfellsnes (1 Night; Book Accommodation)

Reykjavík (1 Night; Book Accommodation)

If your main goal is to see as much as possible, I’d say that late April to mid-October is when you should visit Iceland. My first itinerary is relevant for these months, but it’s better to use it from June to August. While this is the most crowded time of the year, you also have the longest daylight hours. 

One thing I have learned, however, is that visiting Iceland in the summer does not mean you get summer weather 😅. I’ve experienced storms and all sorts even in the warmer months, so you should still be prepared for all conditions. I recommend that you read my packing list to prepare properly, too. 

Should I Self-Cater or Not for This Itinerary?

The choice is yours, but eating out in Iceland is notoriously expensive. I’d recommend having a few splurge meals, but if you want to keep your costs down, self-catering is a good idea. If your hotel only has a fridge, you can at least make sandwiches and keep them in here. I’d also recommend getting protein bars, nuts, dried fruits, and skyr for day trips and hikes. Groceries in Iceland are pricey, but Bónus, Krónan, and Nettó are the three most budget-friendly supermarkets. 

Camping is, of course, also a potential choice in the summer. I have done this before, and I personally quite enjoyed it. Besides the accommodation being cheaper, you can also prepare your own meals. You will, however, need to deal with the drawbacks—such as waiting for showers.

Renting a campervan is a smart idea if you’re going to camp for your 5-day trip to Iceland. Happy Campers is a solid choice, and Kúkú Campers is another option. If you’re looking for places to camp, these are some good campsites:

  • Skaftafell National Park (South Coast)
  • Þingvellir National Park (Golden Circle)
  • Lava Hostel Campsite (Hafnarfjörður, just outside of Reykjavík)
  • Hellissandur (Snæfellsnes)
  • Vík (South Coast)

If you choose to camp in Iceland, you can only stay overnight at designated campsites. Doing so elsewhere is illegal. 

Day 1: Arriving in Iceland and Picking Up Your Rental Car

Total Driving Time: c. 3 Hours

Once you arrive in Iceland, I recommend picking up your rental car from Keflavík International Airport. You can do so after clearing customs and entering the arrivals hall. Rather than first driving to Reykjavík, we’re actually going to go in the opposite direction and head to the South Coast. If you haven’t yet booked your rental car, I recommend comparing your choices with DiscoverCars. For this itinerary, a 2WD should be more than enough. 

Finding your car can sometimes take a while; the rentals area at the airport is huge 😄. Once you’ve done so, though, you can head out toward Vík. This is where you’ll spend the next two nights; I recommend Black Beach Suites, which is just outside the town and one of my all-time favorite places to stay in Iceland.  

You can first of all stop for groceries in Selfoss, but if not, you’ll have another opportunity in Vík. This will largely depend on the time you arrive; the main grocery stores in Selfoss and Vík both close at 21:00. 

Stopping at Some of Iceland’s Most Beautiful Waterfalls

As you continue along the Ring Road, you’ll eventually arrive at Seljalandsfoss. This is about two hours from Keflavík International Airport. While it is one of the more crowded waterfalls in Iceland, I do think it’s worth a stop. You’ll need to pay a parking fee, which you can do when you arrive. 

During the summer, you can walk behind Seljalandsfoss. There is, however, often a queue… so you’ll need to keep this in mind. From here, you can also walk to Gljúfrabúi along the path; it’s hidden behind some rocks. You *will* get wet here, so bring good waterproof equipment and keep your camera protected. Although I think it’s quite overrated, you can still see it if you’re in the area anyway. 

Once you feel like you’ve spent enough time at Seljalandsfoss, you can continue in your car toward Vík. After another 30 minutes or so of driving, you’ll see Skógafoss from the Ring Road. I recommend stopping here, too, and I actually wrote a full guide on visiting this beautiful waterfall. 

Skógafoss is much more powerful than Seljalandsfoss, and it can get crowded when the tour buses are here. You will also need to pay a parking fee when you arrive (this, by the way, will be a recurring theme when you visit the main attractions in Iceland). 

At Skógafoss, I recommend taking the steps up to the top of the waterfall. Walking along some of the trail is also worth your time, in my opinion. We basically walked until we felt like getting back to our car would be too much of an ask. 

Since you’re already at Skógafoss, you might as well also visit Kvernufoss. This is a short drive from Skógafoss, and when you arrive at the parking lot, the walk will take around 30 minutes. Yes, you also need to pay for parking here.

Continuing to Vík

Once you’ve seen these three waterfalls, you’ll have a taste of what’s to come for the rest of your Iceland trip. You’ll probably be a bit tired by now, and I therefore recommend continuing your drive into Vík. It takes around 30 minutes from the Kvernufoss parking lot. 

Like I usually do in the evening with my itineraries, I’m giving you a handful of options when you arrive in Vík. If you want to have a bit of a stroll around Vík, you can go to the church—which has a nice viewpoint of the town and ocean. The Vík Culture Walk is worth doing, too, and Black Crust Pizzeria is a cool place for dinner. 

You can, otherwise, just check into your accommodation and do some grocery shopping before getting a good night’s rest and starting afresh tomorrow. 

📚 Also Worth Reading:

My Favorite Things to Do in (and Around) Vík, Iceland

Day 2: A Day Trip From Vík to Skaftafell National Park

Total Driving Time: c. 4 Hours

Skaftafell National Park is one of my favorite places to visit on Iceland’s South Coast. If you want to see *a lot* of Iceland in a relatively manageable area, it’s perfect. From Vík, Skaftafell is roughly two hours away by car; enter “Skaftafell Parking” into Google Maps. 

The drive from Vík to Skaftafell is pretty cool in some parts, but it can get monotonous in others. You’ll drive between a large moss field and also through sections with large swathes of black sand for miles. However, the drive is quite straightforward; it’s entirely along the Ring Road. 

Before parking, I think it’s worth stopping quickly at the Skeiðará Bridge monument. These twisted metal pieces are the remains of a bridge that was destroyed in a 1996 glacier run. I thought it was pretty interesting, even though many people skip it. 

You’ll also find some spots where you can stop for free with nice views before entering the park, along with picnic benches. 

Once you arrive at Skaftafell National Park, you’ll have to pay a fee (you can do this in the Parka app). You’re then free to explore. 

Skaftafell National Park has several easy hikes that you can do in a day. My personal favorite starts from close to the visitor center and goes along a mostly flat path. We then ended up at an amazing side view of the Svínafellsjökull glacier. We followed the Feysnes/Svínafell sign and basically just walked from there; it took around an hour each way. 

You can also do an easy hike to the view of Skaftafellsjökull, which similarly starts from close to the visitor center. I also enjoyed hiking to the Svartifoss waterfall. For all of these hikes, you’ll find maps for the trails in the national park. 

Depending on how fit and well-rested you are, you could do all three in a day. Otherwise, picking two of these is a good idea. You’ll find a number of other trails with varying difficulties at Skaftafell National Park, too. 

Useful Note: For this day, I recommend bringing some sandwiches and snacks with you. There isn’t really much in terms of food and drink around the national park. 

Day 3: A Long Drive to the Snæfellsnes Peninsula, With Some Pit Stops

Total Driving Time: 6 to 7.5 Hours, depending on detours

Although this day involves a lot of driving, it’s not going to be done in one go. To make it more manageable, I’m breaking everything up into smaller chunks. You’ll have a number of nice pit stops along the way, too, so I promise that it’s worth it. 🙂

Before leaving in the morning, you can go to the Dyrhólaey Nature Reserve if you’re interested. This is quite a nice spot for birdwatching, and the scenery is also beautiful. During the summer, you can spot puffins here, too. 

Otherwise, you can start to make the journey toward Snæfellsnes. On the way, you can make a brief stop at Urriðafoss (Google Maps location here 📍). Nearby Selfoss is a good place to stop for food if you’re hungry, but if not, you’ll have another opportunity along the way to Snæfellsnes. If you stop for food in Selfoss, Tommi’s Burger Joint is pretty good. 

Depending on the weather, you can drive via the Ring Road or Route 360 / Route 36. The Ring Road is more efficient time-wise, but I think that the latter is more scenic. So, if the weather’s good, you might want to consider this option (if it’s not, the Ring Road is a better choice). If you go via Route 360 / Route 36, you could take a quick detour to the Kerið Crater. 

This route also goes close to Þingvellir National Park. You could also take a detour here, but I’d recommend spending at least a few hours, so you’ll need to keep this in mind for your itinerary. If you do, though, Þingvellir is amazing. 

You can then continue to Borgarnes. While there isn’t a huge amount to do in the town, in my opinion, it is a good place to eat and also fuel up the car. If you arrive in time for lunch, the Settlement Center has an excellent vegetarian buffet. So, I’d definitely recommend catching this if you can. 

Continuing to Snæfellsnes

Borgarnes is where the Ring Road splits off for Route 54, which is the main road around the Snæfellsnes Peninsula. I thought a lot about how to properly include the peninsula in this itinerary, because it’s my favorite region in Iceland. An overnight stay is a good idea if you’re self-driving. 

Since you’ve already done a lot of exploring today, we’ll keep things simple for the rest of your afternoon. Definitely stop at Ytri Tunga, which is a great place to see seals. While you’re here, though, beware of the very aggressive Arctic Terns nesting close to the paths.

The iconic black church—Búðakirkja—is relatively close to Ytri Tunga. So, I recommend going here next. The church itself is nice to take photos of, though it’s sometimes annoyingly crowded. My main reason to go here is actually for the hiking trail that starts just behind. We did this hike, which was quite easy and took us a few hours.

If you’ve still got some energy, you can continue to Arnarstapi; it’s a 20-minute drive from Búðakirkja. The walks along the coast here have some of my other favorite views in Iceland, and they’re a must if you enjoy birdwatching. 

I’d recommend staying for the night in Hellissandur, Ólafsvík, or Grundarfjörður. Regardless, the most scenic way to get to any of these towns is via Útnesvegur. Besides great views of Snæfellsjökull, you’ll find a number of spots worth stopping at. When you see a parking lot that interests you, you can make that decision or choose to keep driving. 

Find Accommodation for Your Night on the Snæfellsnes Peninsula:

Day 4: More of Snæfellsnes and Back to Reykjavík

We’ll slowly head back into Reykjavík on this day, but before that, there’s more of the Snæfellsnes Peninsula to see. While I don’t think it’s the *only* reason you should visit, you can’t go to Snæfellsnes without seeing the Kirkjufell mountain. Besides the parking lot viewpoint of the waterfall, which requires a fee, you can see the Game of Thrones mountain from the waterfront in Grundarfjörður. Controversially, I think the mountain itself actually looks more impressive from there. 

You can then either decide to start driving back to Reykjavík and cut in via Route 56, or keep following Route 54. If you’re willing to make a detour, Stykkishólmur is a lovely town that’s worth your time. Depending on what else you want to see, though, it’s okay if you’re short on time and choose to go elsewhere.

By the Way: On the way out of the Snæfellsnes Peninsula, you should also consider stopping for some cakes and coffee at Hjá Goðu Folki (Google Maps location here 📍). 

On your way back to Reykjavík, I actually suggest taking the slower—but more scenic—route. Instead of taking the tunnel, you can drive around Hvalfjörður. I personally think that this fjord is incredibly underrated; we saw almost nobody else here when we visited. 

You can then drive back into Reykjavík within around an hour. Once you arrive in the Icelandic capital, the afternoon is yours to do whatever you want with. You can get plenty of recommendations in my guide on the best things to do in Reykjavík, so be sure to check that out.

Looking for Dinner in Reykjavík? 🍜

My top recommendations would be Tres Locos (Mexican) and Sæta Svínið (Gastropub). For both of these, booking a table in advance is a good idea. 

If you book accommodation anywhere in advance, by the way, it should definitely be Reykjavík. Places fill up fast, especially during the peak season. You can check your options via the map below.

Day 5: Reykjavík

On your final day in Iceland, you can spend it exploring the capital. How much you do will depend on your flight home. If you’re leaving early the day after, you could also consider doing either of these excursions alongside checking out the city:

  • The Reykjavík Food Walk
  • Reykjavík Whale-Watching Tour
  • A Day Tour to the Golden Circle

I’ve also written a complete Reykjavík itinerary for 1-2 days in the city. So, I’d recommend reading that and choosing how you want to spend your day based on the amount of time you’ve got in the capital. 

Itinerary #2: A 5-Day Iceland Itinerary Without a Car

When: Year-Round

Where You’ll Stay: Reykjavík (5 Nights; Book Accommodation)

Although you’ll have less autonomy, you can visit Iceland without a car and have a good time. I have done this a couple of times, and I just accepted the trade-offs that came with it. If you do not plan to rent a car when you visit Iceland, this 5-day itinerary is for you instead. 

For this itinerary, I recommend basing yourself in Reykjavík for the entire trip. Public transport around Iceland is scarce, and flying is not worth it if you’re only in the country for 5 days (plus, it’s very pricey). I wrote a full guide on where to stay in Reykjavík if you want to do some extra research. Otherwise, you can book accommodation below:

Hotels.com

Expedia

These are the tours that I suggest taking in this itinerary, too:

Reykjavík – Golden Circle Day Tour

Reykjavík – Snæfellsnes Day Tour

Reykjavík – South Coast & Jökulsárlón Day Tour

Day 1: Arriving in Iceland & Exploring Reykjavík

Once you arrive in Iceland, you can easily get into Reykjavík from Keflavík International Airport—even without a car. My top suggestion is to book an airport shuttle, which will take you into the city within 45 minutes. It’s not particularly expensive, and you can choose a hotel drop-off as an add-on if you’d like. 

When you arrive in Reykjavík, you can then drop your bags off at your accommodation. For your first day in the city, I mainly suggest taking a walk around the city center. A great first starting point is always the Hallgrímskirkja observation deck, which has the best view over the Icelandic capital. 

In the evening, you can also go for a walk along Sæbraut for some great views of Mount Esja and the bay. From here, it’s easy to reach the Harpa Concert Hall and Tjörnin pond, too. 

If you have more time to spend in the city, you can also read the Reykjavík itinerary that I linked earlier. You may also want to use your first afternoon/evening to do some grocery shopping. 

Day 2: A Day Tour to the Golden Circle

After getting familiar with Reykjavík, I recommend spending your second day in Iceland outside the city. The Golden Circle is one of the most popular places to visit on a first trip to the country, and I’d say that it’s worth it. Even though I have been to Iceland several times now, I still choose to visit the Golden Circle because I simply enjoy it. 

Several tours depart from Reykjavík to the Golden Circle daily. All of them will, at the very least, include Gullfoss, Geysir, and Þingvellir National Park. Others will add the Kerið Crater and different attractions. You can pick the right choice for your own travel needs and preferences. Note that many do not include lunch in their price, but you’ll often have the chance to purchase food. 

Golden Circle Day Tours From Reykjavík:

Since the Golden Circle isn’t too far from Reykjavík, you’ll often have a bit of time to yourself in the evening when you return. If you want to eat out, Íslenski Barinn is a great choice. And yes, you can try fermented shark here. I can confirm that I have done this. 🙂

Day 3: Taking a Day Trip to the Snæfellsnes Peninsula

Although I think that the Snæfellsnes Peninsula is best explored on an overnight trip, you need a car if you want to do that. If you aren’t driving, taking a day tour from Reykjavík is a viable alternative. I’ve actually done this before, and it was worth it to at least see the main sights. My top recommendation is the tour below:

The Snæfellsnes peninsula is a bit further away from Reykjavík than the Golden Circle, so your day will typically start earlier. You can choose where you want to be picked up, and you’ll generally be out of the city for the full day. Each tour will take you to the likes of Kirkjufell, but they’ll differ in terms of group sizes and other offerings. For example, some will include lunch, but others won’t. 

Much of your day will be sightseeing rather than hiking, but you should still dress appropriately. It can get *very* windy in this part of Iceland, to say the least. Like the Golden Circle, you have plenty of day tour options to choose from. 

More Snæfellsnes Day Tours:

Day 4: A Day Tour to the South Coast

One advantage of taking a day tour to the South Coast versus driving it yourself is that with a day tour, you can cover much more distance in a single day. I always strongly advise against trying to do a day trip to the South Coast if you’re self-driving. On the flip side, though, taking a day tour to the South Coast was one of my all-time top Iceland tour experiences. 

Most of the South Coast day tours from Reykjavík will be very, very long days. But you will see a lot, and it definitely won’t feel boring. Pretty much all of them will cover the likes of Seljalandsfoss and Skógafoss. Sadly, you won’t get to see too much of Skaftafell National Park in many cases, but it is what it is. Some tours will go all the way to Jökulsárlón (the Glacier Lagoon), but this isn’t always the case. 

You can pick whether you want to take a small-group South Coast tour, like this one, or other options if you don’t mind so much. If you want one that does include Jökulsárlón, you can have a look at this option instead. 

More South Coast Day Tours & Excursions:

Day 5: Two Options

For your fifth day on this trip, you can either stay in Reykjavík. If you do that, you can decide if you want to explore more of the city. You should definitely start your day with some pastries from Brauð & Co., in that case… these are some of the best in the Nordics, and I say this as someone who has “done a lot of research”. 

For the rest of your day, you can take it easy and go between the city’s many cafés, galleries, and museums. If you want to get out a bit more, you can also take a whale-watching tour. 

Another option is to relax at the nearby Sky Lagoon. This is one of my favorite spas in Iceland, and it’s up against some stiff competition in that respect. It’s a short bus ride from Downtown Reykjavík, and if you want to take things really easy, the Sky Lagoon is the perfect place to relax. I suggest buying your tickets in advance.

You can generally stay as long as you want at the Sky Lagoon, unless it’s particularly busy. I’d recommend spending around 2-3 hours here. Once you’ve done that, you can head back into Reykjavík and explore the city some more (or head to the airport if you have a flight to catch).

Itinerary #3: A 5-Day Winter Itinerary

When: November to March

Where You’ll Stay: Reykjavík (1 night), Vík (1 night), Reykjavík (2-3 nights)

I’ve created a completely separate winter itinerary because visiting Iceland at this time of the year is very different. The daylight hours are very short, and by that, I mean that Reykjavík only has four hours of daylight on the shortest day of the year in December. The weather is also cold, wet, and windy, often at the same time. 

If you’re visiting without a car, you can follow the previous itinerary I mentioned. If not, this 5-day itinerary is a realistic idea of what you can see and do when visiting Iceland during the winter. 

Before We Start: Some Useful Tips for This Winter Itinerary ❄️

Car Rentals: Your rental car should be fitted with winter tires, and a 2WD should be fine for this route. However, if you want to be on the safer side, you can always rent a 4WD instead. You can browse options on DiscoverCars. 

When you’re in Reykjavík, I recommend parking your car at the Harpa Concert Hall parking lot. This is much easier than trying to find a space right in the city center. 

Flexibility: You need to be prepared to change your itinerary, even more so than in the summer. Iceland’s weather is even more unpredictable in the winter, and storms are common. So, I suggest treating this itinerary as a guideline rather than a hard-line rule. 

Accommodation: You’ll mainly stay in Reykjavík for this itinerary, along with one night in Vík on the South Coast. 

You can book accommodation for Reykjavík here. 

As for Vík, you can find places to stay here. 

Northern Lights Hunting: I recommend joining a guided tour if you want to see the Northern Lights. Many providers let you rebook if you don’t see them. You can browse the best Northern Lights tours in Iceland here. 

Day 1: Reykjavík

Driving Time: 45 minutes

From Keflavík Airport, I suggest picking up your rental car and driving into Reykjavík. The journey takes around 45 minutes. What you do when you arrive will depend largely on the time you visit and when the sunset is. You’ll have more flexibility toward the end of the winter season. 

Winter is actually my favorite time to visit Reykjavík, and it’s a great place to start your trip if you plan to visit during the colder months. Iceland’s capital looks beautiful if you have a clear day and soft lighting, though it’s often admittedly quite gray and damp. A trip to the top of Hallgrímskirkja is an absolute must, especially if the city is under a layer of snow. 

You can then go for a bit of a stroll around the city before heading to Sæta Svínið for some food and drinks. The lamb and burgers here are great, and you’ll find plenty of beers on tap, too. If it’s particularly cold or stormy outside, this is a good place to hide from the elements. 

Depending on the time, you can also check out the snow-covered Mount Esja from Sæbraut. This, coupled with a pink sky, is one of my favorite sights on the entire planet. I then recommend having more of a walk around Reykjavík before heading into the city for dinner. Tres Locos is a solid option for the first day of your winter trip. 

Day 2: A Road Trip to Vík

Total Driving Time: 2.5 hours

Unless you have much longer, or you’re planning to take a day tour, I do not recommend trying to do the full South Coast on a 5-day winter trip to Iceland. However, you can at least see some of the main highlights. So, on your second day, I will suggest heading down to Vík to spend a night. 

Given the short daylight hours, I’d recommend leaving an hour or two before sunrise. The drive from Reykjavík to Vík gets more scenic as you head further away from Reykjavík, and as such, it’s better to be further down the coast by this time. 

Worth Noting: The drive to Vík goes along the Ring Road, which is generally well-maintained. However, you should still watch out for ice and keep in mind potential hazards like crosswinds. Checking road conditions before you leave is also a good idea.  

On your way to Vík, I recommend stopping at Seljalandsfoss and Skógafoss. Seljalandsfoss is first. While you cannot walk behind the waterfall during the winter, it is still worth seeing. The crowds are also significantly smaller than in the summer, and in my opinion, the waterfall looks even nicer in the colder months. 

You can then continue on to Skógafoss. Like Seljalandsfoss, the crowds will generally be thinner during the winter. It’s a great place for photography at this time of the year, too, which is a nice bonus. 

From Skógafoss, it’s a short drive to Vík. Here, you can spend the bulk of your afternoon in the town. It’s pretty small, and you can easily see it in one day. Given that the sun will be going down at this point, you can then head to your accommodation for the evening or into Vík for some dinner. 

Find Accommodation for the Night in Vík:

Day 3: Back to Reykjavík, Plus Northern Lights Hunting

Driving Time: 2.5 hours

While one night is nowhere near enough to see the entire South Coast, you will have at least gotten a taste of it. For the third day of this winter itinerary, I recommend taking the drive back into Reykjavík early in the morning. You can stop in Selfoss for lunch along the way and also check out the New Old Town while you’re here. 

In the afternoon, you can then spend some more time exploring Reykjavík. Whether you choose the same hotel that you stayed in before, or another one, is up to you. If you haven’t already, I’d recommend using this time to explore the neighborhoods behind Tjörnin and the Old Harbor, too. Here, you can go for an early dinner. 

Later in the evening, I’d recommend trying to go Northern Lights hunting. When I did this, it was particularly cold… but we also maxed out on our luck and got an amazing show. It was worth the trip, and we had somewhere nice to chill out in the meantime, too. 

You can choose from several Northern Lights tours. Some will include extra niceties like hot drinks and photos, and you can browse from multiple options below. 

Day 4: Reykjavík to the Golden Circle

Driving Time: c. 6 hours

Okay, so this will be one of the longer days on this itinerary. If you’re visiting Iceland in December or January, when the days are particularly short, I recommend leaving Reykjavík no later than 90 minutes before sunrise. I also suggest packing your own food for this day, with plenty of snacks. 

While on the Golden Circle, you should—in my opinion—allocate most of your time to Þingvellir National Park. By that, I mean at least 2 hours, if you can. 

You can walk between the North American and Eurasian tectonic plates year-round, and this should definitely be one of your top priorities. Whether you can do some of the hikes in the park will depend on the weather; for example, while we went to Öxarárfoss toward the end of winter, the trail was passable but slippery in parts. I would recommend at least having a bit of a walk around as much as you can. 

Geysir is around a 35-minute drive from Þingvellir National Park, and you don’t need to spend too much time here. Around 25-30 minutes is enough; watching the geysers erupt is cool, but in my opinion, there isn’t a huge amount of other things to do around there. 

Gullfoss is then roughly 25 minutes from Geysir by car. This is one of my favorite waterfalls in Iceland, and even though I’ve been there multiple times, I still enjoy going back each time. You’ll also find a café here if you want to buy a meal and some sweet treats, and also if you just want to shelter from the cold a bit. 

While on the Golden Circle, you can also—if the conditions are good enough—take a detour to the Kerið Crater. We spent around 40 minutes here, and when we visited, the middle of the crater was frozen. I personally thought it was quite an interesting place to visit, so it’s worth potentially adding to your itinerary. 

It’ll take you around an hour to get back into Reykjavík after you’ve completed the Golden Circle. Depending on when you arrive, you can then go for dinner in the city or back to your hotel. And if you want to try some of the city’s bars, you should definitely stop by Skúli Craft Bar on Aðalstræti, in my opinion. 

Day 5: Spend Some Extra Time Exploring Reykjavík

On the final day of your winter trip in Iceland, you can choose to spend some extra time exploring Reykjavík. Even if you have an early afternoon flight, you can still get some walking in during the morning. My personal favorite activity is to just go for an aimless walk, while occasionally dipping in and out of the many great bakeries and cafés. 

Otherwise, depending on how much time you have, you can go and relax at the Sky Lagoon. You can drive from Downtown Reykjavík in less than 20 minutes, and you can book your tickets here.

Another option is to go to the Blue Lagoon, which is quite close to Keflavík Airport. I personally prefer the Sky Lagoon, but the Blue Lagoon was worth visiting at least once. The restaurant here is also very good, and you’ll even find a hotel here if you’d like to stay overnight before your flight. 

Blue Lagoon Tickets & Combos:

Even if You Only Have 5 Days in Iceland, You Can Still Have a Great Time

Although you won’t see all of Iceland in just 5 days, you can still have an amazing trip. I also have actually enjoyed some of my shorter stays more, where I’ve only seen a few regions in the country but done so more deeply. Moreover, these trips are often the most relaxed, with a mixture of sightseeing, spas, and hiking. 

How you spend this amount of time in the country will vary depending on when you visit, but also on whether you rent a car. You’ll have much more flexibility in the summer, but at the same time, winter is also an amazing time to visit. Now that you’ve read this guide, you should have a better idea of what to do when you arrive in the country. 

If you have any further questions, you’re more than welcome to leave a comment. I’ll do what I can to help. And if you want to plan your trip even further, be sure to check out my recommendations for the absolute best things to do in Iceland.
